E1.source: Greenhouse irrigation timers are usually programmed once at installation and rarely revisited as crops mature or weather changes. Growers at the Ashford Ridge cooperative had also never compared their schedules against runoff records, which made the trial possible. The principal finding is that moving the morning irrigation start from 5:00 to 6:30 reduced substrate runoff by 23 percent across the fourteen bays monitored during the eight-week trial. The evidence has a clear limit: readings came from one growing season, and the moisture loggers were recalibrated only twice, so sensor drift cannot be excluded as a contributor. The scope is also narrow, since the results apply only to tomato and cucumber bays under passive ventilation and say nothing about hydroponic or heated structures. Before any grower changes a timer based on this note, they should confirm that their substrate moisture sensors agree within two percent of a gravimetric check taken on the same day.
E1.good: Moving the morning irrigation start from 5:00 to 6:30 cut substrate runoff 23% across fourteen monitored bays in an eight-week trial at Ashford Ridge. Limits: one season, sensors recalibrated only twice (drift not excluded), and applies only to tomato and cucumber bays under passive ventilation. Before changing timers, confirm moisture sensors agree within 2% of a same-day gravimetric check.
E1.bad: Moving the morning irrigation start from 5:00 to 6:30 cut substrate runoff by 23 percent across fourteen bays, so growers can expect the same reduction. The trial ran for eight weeks, and sensor drift cannot be excluded. Before changing timers, check that moisture sensors agree with a same-day gravimetric test.
E1.why_bad: It drops the scope limit (tomato and cucumber bays under passive ventilation only, with nothing said about hydroponic or heated structures) and strengthens the finding into a result growers can expect.

E2.source: Field review of the Harbor Point parcel-locker bank, unit cluster B, found that the door sensor failed to register closure in 17 of 240 compartment cycles sampled over six weeks, a fault rate of about 7.1 percent. Most failures clustered in the mornings, when humidity inside the enclosure was highest and the magnetic reed contacts showed visible condensation residue. Technicians at the Ferrow Lane depot, which maintains the bank under a contract with the fictional operator Lindqvist Terminals, attributed the pattern to seal degradation rather than wiring faults, though no teardown was performed. The sample covered only one bank in one climate zone, so the rate may not hold for lockers installed in drier or sheltered sites. The review also did not test the newer capacitive sensor model, which the operator is evaluating for the next procurement cycle. Before any sensor replacement is ordered, the operator should confirm that the seal failure reproduces under controlled humidity testing, since a repeat of the morning pattern would support the seal explanation and a different pattern would not.
E2.good: A field review of Harbor Point parcel-locker cluster B found the door sensor failed to register closure in 17 of 240 cycles (about 7.1%) over six weeks, mostly in mornings when humidity and condensation on the reed contacts peaked. Technicians blamed seal degradation, but no teardown was done. The sample covered one bank in one climate, and the newer capacitive sensor was not tested. Before ordering replacements, confirm the seal failure reproduces under controlled humidity testing.
E2.bad: The Harbor Point door sensor fails in about 7.1 percent of compartment cycles, so the rate applies across the operator's locker network. Technicians blamed seal degradation, though no teardown was performed. Before ordering replacements, confirm the seal failure reproduces under controlled humidity testing.
E2.why_bad: It drops the scope limits (one bank in one climate zone, and the newer capacitive sensor model was not tested) and strengthens the finding into a rate that applies across the whole locker network.

E3.source:
Internal technical note, Brightwater Transport Analytics, file ref. BTA-RN-0417

Background: The Eastfield district adopted the Larkspur routing engine in 2024 after a pilot that the board later judged too brief to settle questions about winter operations. Drivers were not consulted during the original design, and their informal adjustments to stop order were never recorded, which is part of why the current comparison is harder to read than it looks.

Over the autumn term, the optimiser cut total daily mileage across the fourteen Eastfield routes by 11.2 percent, from 1,846 to 1,639 miles, while keeping every student's pickup within the 0.8-mile walking limit. The reduction was largest on the two northern loops, where overlapping stops had previously been served twice. That is the principal finding, and it holds for the weekday schedule as modelled.

The first qualification is that the evidence comes from simulated trips built on enrolment records from September. Actual traffic delays, road closures, and student absences were not measured, so the mileage figure is a model output rather than a fleet log. The second is that the study covers only the Eastfield district and only the morning and afternoon runs; the Coldharbour and Millbrook depots, and any late or activity buses, fall outside it. The third is a condition: before any route is changed, the transport office must confirm with the safeguarding lead that no student's new stop lies outside the agreed supervised-catchment boundaries, because the optimiser does not check this constraint.
E3.good: Eastfield's Larkspur routing engine cut simulated daily mileage across 14 routes by 11.2% (1,846 to 1,639 miles) while keeping walks within 0.8 miles. Caveats: results come from simulated September enrolment data, not fleet logs; only Eastfield morning and afternoon runs were studied. Before any route change, confirm with the safeguarding lead that new stops stay within supervised catchment boundaries, since the optimiser doesn't check this.
E3.bad: Eastfield's Larkspur routing engine cut simulated mileage across 14 routes by 11.2% while keeping every walk within 0.8 miles. The model used September enrolment data and covers Eastfield's morning and afternoon runs. A live pilot on the Coldharbour depot later confirmed these savings. Before any route change, confirm with the safeguarding lead that new stops stay inside supervised boundaries.
E3.why_bad: It invents a completed live pilot at the Coldharbour depot that confirmed the savings, which the note never reports and places outside the study.
